cards.bodyHtml: Full wave gives twice the average output of half wave and a ripple at twice the line frequency, so it needs less filtering.

cards.title: Clippers and clampers
cards.bodyHtml: A clipper removes part of the waveform; a clamper shifts the whole waveform by charging a series capacitor to a DC level. A clamper preserves the peak-to-peak swing.

topics.title: BJT and MOSFET Amplifiers
topics.syllabus: BJT and MOSFET Amplifiers: Biasing, AC coupling, small signal analysis, frequency response. Current mirrors and differential amplifiers.

cards.title: The three configurations
cards.bodyHtml: Pick by impedance, not by gain. Common source/emitter inverts and gives voltage gain; common drain/collector is a buffer; common gate/base is a current buffer with low input impedance.

cards.bodyHtml: A resistor in the source or emitter trades gain for linearity and raises input and output impedance. It is negative feedback in its simplest form.

cards.title: Current mirrors and diff pairs
cards.bodyHtml: A mirror copies a reference current, scaled by the device ratio. A differential pair splits a fixed tail current between two branches according to the input difference.

cards.title: Biasing and AC coupling
cards.bodyHtml: Biasing sets the Q-point; coupling keeps it there while the signal passes through. The whole art is making the operating point depend on resistor ratios — which are stable — rather than on β\betaβ or VBEV_{BE}VBE​, which vary between devices and with temperature.
cards.pitfallHtml: Coupling and bypass capacitors set the low-frequency roll-off; device and wiring capacitances set the high-frequency one. Attributing a high-frequency fall to the coupling capacitor is the classic wrong answer — and one of the answer keys in this bank gets it wrong that way.

topics.title: Op-amp Circuits
topics.syllabus: Op-amp Circuits: Amplifiers, summers, differentiators, integrators, active filters, Schmitt triggers and oscillators.

cards.title: The two golden rules
cards.bodyHtml: With negative feedback present, no current enters the inputs and the two input terminals sit at the same voltage. Almost every linear op-amp question falls out of these two facts plus KCL at the inverting node.
cards.pitfallHtml: With positive feedback — a Schmitt trigger — the virtual short does not hold; the output is at a rail.

cards.bodyHtml: Where the capacitor sits decides which one it is: in the feedback path it integrates, in the input path it differentiates.

cards.bodyHtml: Positive feedback gives two switching thresholds, and the gap between them is the hysteresis that rejects noise.

cards.title: Summers, difference and instrumentation amplifiers
cards.bodyHtml: All of these follow from the virtual short and no input current. A summing amplifier is just several inputs meeting at the virtual ground, so each contributes independently of the others — which is what makes weighted-resistor DACs work.

cards.title: Active filters
cards.bodyHtml: An op-amp lets an RCRCRC network be cascaded without loading the previous stage, so the order adds up cleanly. Recognise the topology first: feedback through a capacitor is a low pass (an integrator), a capacitor in the input path is a high pass.
cards.pitfallHtml: An ideal integrator has infinite DC gain and saturates on any input offset. The practical one puts a large resistor across the feedback capacitor — and that resistor is why it stops integrating below 1/2πRfC1/2\pi R_fC1/2πRf​C.
